ordering: Unattributed rows first (12 of them), then by longest run descending.

rows_detail.proposed: Where work happens in an online environment rather than a place - model registries, pipelines, cloud estates, logging platforms. Clause 3.6 notes that audit scope covers virtual locations as well as physical ones, which matters because most of an AI management system's evidence lives nowhere you can walk to.

Clause 9.3.3 wants the review to produce decisions - on improvement opportunities and on any changes the AIMS needs - and documented evidence of them. A review minuted with attendance and discussion but no decision has not produced what the clause asks for.

Clause 6.1.4 makes the connection a shall and gives it a direction: impact findings go into the risk assessment. Two sound documents sitting side by side satisfy nothing - the evidence is the impact conclusions appearing in the risk record.

Auditors are to be chosen and audits run so that objectivity and impartiality hold. Clause 9.2.2. That one sentence is everything ISO/IEC 27001 says about auditor independence - there is no separation-of-duties rule and no prohibition to find.

Clause 7.5.2 governs how documented information is made: identified and described, in a fit format, reviewed and approved. Clause 7.5.3 governs what happens next - available where needed, and protected. Existence is not control: a current model card nobody approved and anyone can overwrite satisfies neither.

Family A.6 covers the AI system life cycle - responsible development, the processes themselves, verification and validation, deployment, operation and monitoring, technical documentation and event logging. Some of its controls set their own floor: A.6.2.6 asks what ongoing operation needs and names monitoring, repairs, updates and support as the minimum.

Internal audits at planned intervals, asking two things: whether the ISMS meets the organization's own requirements and the standard's, and whether it is actually operating. Clause 9.2.1. Conformity and effective implementation are separate questions, and an audit answering only the first is incomplete.

Clause 7.2 runs in four steps: work out what competence the work needs, confirm the people have it through education, training or experience, act where they do not and check the action worked, and keep the evidence. A job title evidences none of it.

Table A.1 groups its controls into nine families, each carrying a stated objective - policies, internal organization, resources, impact assessment, life cycle, data, information for interested parties, use, and third-party relationships. The objective is what an exclusion has to be justified against, which is why it matters more than the list.

Clause 4.3 asks for the boundaries and applicability of the ISMS, weighed against the 4.1 issues, the 4.2 requirements, and the interfaces and dependencies with other organizations. The scope is documented information, and the interfaces are where a scope statement usually stops describing reality.

Clause 6.3 says that once the organization decides the ISMS needs changing, the change has to be carried out in a planned manner. It is routinely missed because it does not appear on the standard's own contents page.

Documentation showing that a system does what it is required to do - not that it was built, but that the requirements are met. The distinction decides whether a build record counts as evidence at all.

Clause 1 Scope, not clause 4, is where this sits: an organization claiming conformity cannot exclude any requirement from clauses 4 to 10. Activities, locations and assets can fall outside a scope boundary; requirements cannot, and confusing the two is the usual error.

Clause 5.2 puts the programme's objectives on the audit client, and ties them to the organization's strategic direction and its management system policies. It lists what they can rest on - interested parties' expectations, the management system's own requirements, the auditee's performance, and the need to evaluate the supply chain.

Clause 6.1.2 obliges a defined AI risk assessment process with named properties: aligned to the AI policy and objectives, repeatable enough to give consistent and comparable results, and able to identify, analyse and evaluate risks to the AI objectives. The requirement is on the process, not on any one assessment.

Annex A.1 says the organization need not use every control in Table A.1 and may design its own. So a Table A.1 shall is conditional: it binds whoever determined that control necessary and declared it. Saying ISO/IEC 42001 requires an AI policy control misstates that; saying where A.2.2 is selected the organization shall document an AI policy does not.

Clause 7.2.3 item 10 puts a competence on the auditor: understanding what audit tooling does to an audit, and what follows from using it. It is written generally - remote-audit platforms, sampling and analysis software, and whatever arrives next are all inside it.

Clause 3.1 defines an audit as a systematic, independent, documented process for gathering objective evidence and judging it against criteria. Note 2 adds that an internal audit is done by or for the organization itself - so a contracted auditor still yields a first-party audit. What makes it internal is whose management system is examined, not who holds the pen.

Clause 5.5.2 asks each audit to carry its own objectives, scope and criteria, consistent with the programme's. It names what those objectives can be: extent of conformity, capability to meet statutory and regulatory requirements, effectiveness against intended results, and opportunities to improve.

Control A.4.6 asks the organization to record who works on the AI system life cycle and what competences they hold, across development, deployment, operation, change, maintenance and transfer. Where selected, it produces exactly the record that clause 7.2's competence determination can be read against.

Clause 10.2 sets a sequence: react to the nonconformity and deal with its consequences, then decide whether the cause needs eliminating - and if so review it, find the cause, and ask where else that cause operates. Then act, check the action worked, and change the AIMS if needed. That third element, where else, is the one most often skipped.

Clause 9.3.1 puts periodic review on top management, testing continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness. 9.3.2 fixes what goes in and 9.3.3 what must come out, with evidence of the results. Three subclauses, so a review can satisfy one and fail another.

Conducting audit activities from anywhere other than where the auditee is. Clause 3.4, imported into the 2026 edition from ISO/IEC TS 17012:2024 along with its guidance. The definition turns on location, not on technology.

Records, statements of fact or other information that bear on the criteria and can be checked. Clause 3.10. Both halves are load-bearing: something relevant but unverifiable is not evidence, and neither is something verifiable but beside the point.

Annex A.16 accepts that remote methods bring their own risks and opportunities. What it does not change is the test in Annex A.5: complete, correct, consistent, current, and integrity assessable. The method moves; the standard of sufficiency does not.

Annex A.16 notes that auditing remotely introduces risks as well as opportunities, naming data security, confidentiality, and planning for the technology failing. They are considerations to weigh, not reasons to refuse the method.

Clause 6.1.2 b) makes repeatability a property the process must have. It is testable: two people assessing similar systems from the same facts and reaching materially different conclusions is evidence the process fails it - and the evidence is the organization's own assessment records.
